title: Wait for the most common diagnostic scans in Manitoba 'worse now than it ever has been': doctor
summary: Doctors and patients say a diagnostic wait time crisis is putting people's lives at risk, as the highest number of Manitobans on record wait for scans that help diagnose brain tumours, heart disease…

blocks.text: Doctors and patients say a diagnostic wait time crisis is putting people's lives at risk, as the highest number of Manitobans on record wait for scans that help diagnose brain tumours, heart disease and other potentially deadly medical conditions.
The number of people waiting for CT scans and ultrasounds in the province now surpasses the wait caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the province's diagnostic wait time data.
Over 45,000 people in the province were waiting for an ultrasound as of August 2026, compared to an average of 16,000 in 2019 — the furthest back the province's publicly available data goes.
Almost 29,000 were waiting for a CT scan in August (up from 8,000 in 2019), and 18,000 for an MRI (up from 15,000).
"It is worse now than it ever has been," said Dr. Fourie Smith, a family physician who has practised in Manitoba since 1998.

Earlier this month, Winnipeg comedian Big Daddy Tazz paid for a private magnetic resonance imaging test, which creates images of structures inside the body, after he was told he would likely wait a year for a spine MRI to help diagnose pain that was shooting up his arms and legs.
"I was afraid if I didn't pay for this MRI, that if we were on the wrong track and I did the wrong thing for a year, that I would do more damage," he said.

blocks.text: The standup comedian paid $950 for a private MRI in Kelowna, B.C, where he has a second home.

He learned he has a pinched nerve tunnel in his spine and a condition that was putting pressure on his spinal cord. He doesn't need surgery, but the test gave him a path for how to treat his pain through stretches and exercise.
Without the test, "for another year, I would've waited for the results, to find out that I could be doing something to relieve myself of some of the pain," he said.
Big Daddy Tazz paid $950 for a private MRI, a medical imaging test that creates images of structures inside the body. (CBC)

A CBC analysis of the province's diagnostic wait time data found that depending on where the scan is sent, Manitobans can wait nine months or longer for an ultrasound, 15 months for a CT scan and 10 months for an MRI.

Manitoba family doctors say those waits are putting them at a breaking point, where they struggle to make the best medical decisions for their patients when the answer is reliant on a diagnostic image that could take a year to receive.
Demand outpaces staffing: union
The province tracks the median number of weeks a person waits for a scan from the time a requisition is sent to a facility to when it was completed.

At Grace Hospital, the median wait for a CT scan is over a year, according to the Winnipeg hospital's August data. That means half the people waited less than a year for a CT and the other half waited longer.
At Misericordia Health Centre in Winnipeg, patients waited nine months for an ultrasound.
While the MRI waitlist has improved from 2025, when times ballooned and over 28,000 people were on the list, patients are still consistently waiting 10 months or longer.
Dr. Michel Bruneau, a family doctor in Lac du Bonnet, says he sometimes won't even bother ordering an MRI because he knows the wait will make it useless. (Gary Solilak/CBC)
Dr. Michel Bruneau, a family physician in Lac du Bonnet, northeast of Winnipeg, said he often just skips ordering an MRI, because he knows the wait will be so long the test won't be of any use.
"By the time they get their [scan], the damage is done, and you can't do anything about it anyway if you wait six months," he said.
Since 2019, the average number of CT scans done in the province has increased by 38 per cent, while MRIs have increased by 23 per cent and ultrasounds by 11 per cent.
But the union that represents the technologists needed to do those scans says staffing rates have not kept pace.

blocks.text: The number of full-time equivalent technologist positions has only slightly increased since 2019, according to the Manitoba Association of Health Care Professionals. Union president Jason Linklater says it's time for Manitoba's NDP government, in office since 2023, to create a human resources strategy to meet the demand.

Dayna McTaggart, the Manitoba provincial manager with the Canadian Association of Medical Radiation Technologists, says the increased demand for scans stems from an aging population, increased disease monitoring and more patients with family physicians.

Dayna McTaggart, the provincial manager of the Canadian Association of Medical Radiation Technologists of Manitoba, says the demand for diagnostic imaging has been steadily increasing. (Submitted by Dayna McTaggart)
The association warned governments that increase was coming for years, yet "we haven't seen an equal increase in the growth of the profession," said McTaggart.
Manitoba Health Minister Uzoma Asagwara echoed McTaggart's point on doctors, saying that because the province has hired more physicians, there will be more referrals.

The solution is "to train the right number of people to deliver these tests and scans," the minister said, pointing to a mobile MRI unit that recently moved to The Pas to start doing testing in northern Manitoba.
'Crisis for physicians': Doctors Manitoba
Dr. Smith, who is the medical director of Winnipeg's Dakota Medical Centre, said the situation has become so dire he is constantly forced to decide which of his patients he can help move up the list.
He can only ask radiologists for a priority slot so many times, he said.
"Imagine being put in that position where I have to decide between case A, B and C, when I'm going to pick up the phone and make that call," he said.
The doctor said he can’t pinpoint exactly when things got so bad, but said it began in the last two years.

items: MRI waits surge in Manitoba after nearly 2 years of NDP governance

blocks.text: The province proactively publishes a wait times dashboard that gives an average median wait time for procedures, using data from all facilities. That means in calculating median wait times, the nine-week wait for an MRI for a child at Health Sciences Centre is given the same weight as the 10-month wait for an adult MRI at HSC.
Those median times also do not capture how long it can take for the scan ordered by the doctor to be processed by the province's central intake system and put in the queue.
That can extend the wait by up to three months or longer, say Dr. Smith and Doctors Manitoba — the advocacy association that represents over 4,000 physicians.
The intake system used by Shared Health, Manitoba's provincial health agency, relies on a digital fax system.
That means "if we say that the wait times in Manitoba is X, it's actually significantly worse than that, because that referral lies. … waiting to get processed," Dr. Smith said.
Doctors Manitoba surveyed 68 physicians who said 78 per cent of their requisitions take over a month to get acknowledged by intake.
Manitoba government urged to tackle record diagnostic wait times
One doctor noted a requisition took six months to process before it was rejected for missing details. Others reported requisitions going missing.
More than 60 per cent of the doctors surveyed said the increased wait worsened patient outcomes through delayed diagnoses, poorer health and additional required treatments.
The combination of long waits for tests and the central intake bottleneck have created a "crisis for physicians trying to get their patients the care they need," a Doctors Manitoba spokesperson said.
Central intake has a 24-hour turnaround for urgent scans, but is still processing non-urgent requisitions from August, said a spokesperson for Shared Health.
Minister Asagwara said they recently attended a Doctors Manitoba summit on the issues with the referral process, and they are committed to "axe the fax."

Work is ongoing to modernize the central intake system, Shared Health's spokesperson said in an emailed statement. A casual clerical staffer has been hired to help address outstanding requisitions, they said.
'Not just a number on a piece of paper'
But Smith said the current situation leaves doctors, who have no way of tracking the status of their referrals, wanting "to pull our hair out" with frustration.

There were at least two cases where his office waited a year to hear about a referral and was told by central intake it was sent to a hospital, only for the hospital to say they never received it, said Smith.

Lac du Bonnet's Dr. Bruneau said he sees the consequences of the wait times with his dementia patients. A brain CT scan can help diagnose the cause of the dementia and lead to treatment — but waiting a year delays the ability to do that.
"In that year, that person with dementia has often declined significantly," he said.

Big Daddy Tazz said he grapples with what he describes as survivor's guilt because he got an MRI immediately, knowing many others can't afford that option. That's one reason he's speaking up, he said.
"This needs addressing," said Tazz. People on waitlists need to know the province cares, he said.
"We're not just a number on a piece of paper. We are human beings that are terrified."
